This might and probably does come off as a pretty strange and stupid question but I was listening to a video a couple weeks back that was saying gravity isn't actually a force but rather just that everything sorts itself by density. At the time I didn't think much of it but the thoughts been crossing my mind recently so I figured I'd ask other peoples opinions on it.

I'm not denying things don't fall but that gravity itself could just be a flawed theory. Whenever they try to explain gravity they use the example of a bowling ball on a trampoline saying it represents mass warping spacetime but the fact they're using gravity to explain gravity doesn't actually explain anything at all. Also things such as the high tide though being said to be caused by the moon's gravitational pull occurs twice a day practically refuting the moon as being the cause of it.

Put a handful of different liquids in a jar and they aren't mixed and all pulled down equally by gravity but rather sort themselves out based upon density. http://i.imgur.com/15hIt1r.jpg

isn't actually a force but rather just that everything sorts itself by density.

How would that work in space?

But gravity is understood and proven. The jar example is just density (the denser/heavier fluids go to the bottom, and the lighter stay on top).

Also things such as the high tide though being said to be caused by the moon's gravitational pull occurs twice a day practically refuting the moon as being the cause of it.

Here's a useful schematic.

The force of gravity diminishes with distance, so everything closer to the Moon gets pulled on more than anything that's further away. Closest to the moon, you have the water being pulled up towards it. Then when you get further away, it's the Earth itself that's being pulled towards the Moon, leaving the water on the other side further away. This causes high tide on opposite sides of the planet, with low tide in between. The Earth itself undergoes tidal effects as well, deforming a bit.

That makes no sense why gravity (which pulls) would push water to bulge up on the opposite side of the planet.. Does gravity have that much of an adverse effect over the 8,000 mile diameter of Earth when it's coming 250,000 miles from it's source?

A good example of what is happening is if you were playing with your son/daughter/niece/nephew/whatever and you picked this child up by the arms and started spinning him/her around you. Just as his arms are pulled toward you by the force you are applying to his arms his legs are being kicked away from you. Now imagine this child's arms as the near side tide his body as the planetary body and the legs as the far side tide.

Now, just as we, the earth, are causing these tidal forces on the moon, the moon is causing a lessened version of the same force here on earth that we can easily see as the tides of the ocean.
It is well understood what gravity does but not why. If yo figure that out, you'll get the biggest Nobel prize of all. BTW, don't compare gravity with density.
Very easy to prove gravity's effects, but no one has an answer to why is there gravity.

Is there proof of gravity?

Yes, electrically and magnetically neutral objects fall toward a very massive object. But gravity isn't the only force. The electric and magnetic forces also operate. How do small rocks and dust cling to small asteroids and comets in space? It's surely due to static electric charge. The gravity of such small objects is way too weak to hold anything down on them.

The tides are also due to static electric force. This paper explains it http://qdl.scs-inc.us/?top=6199

But is gravity a pull or a push? It seems to be inconceivable that attractive forces are real in physics. A push makes sense. You can throw a ball at another ball and make the first one push the other one away. But a pull doesn't make obvious sense. How can you attract the second ball toward you? You'd have to throw the first ball at a backstop and make it bounce back and hit the second ball to make it come toward you.

High and low pressure makes sense. So it's more plausible that gravity may be a push from some kind of high pressure area toward a low pressure area. Maybe the pressure comes from invisible light or something like that.
